generalizedRange: Northeast Brazil — the Caatinga of northern Bahia along the São Francisco river; no free-living birds today
hook: Gone from the wild in 2000. Back in 2022. Recaptured in 2025.

story.text: Spix’s macaw is a small blue macaw of Brazil’s Caatinga, 55 to 57 centimeters long, bare grey skin around a mustard-yellow eye.
Its last wild population lived in caraibeira gallery woodland along seasonal creeks near Curaçá, Bahia, nesting in the trees’ hollows.
Clearing of that woodland, then trapping for the cage-bird trade in the 1970s and 80s, left a single wild bird by 1990.
It was last seen in October 2000; in 2019 the Red List moved the species to Extinct in the Wild.
Captive breeding carried it: 152 birds by 2017, and in 2020 fifty-two were flown home to Brazil’s new breeding and reintroduction center.
Twenty were released into the Caatinga in 2022; 58 percent survived the first year, and in May 2024 two wild-hatched chicks flew.
That June, Brazil’s ICMBio let its agreement with the German breeder ACTP lapse over a disputed transfer of birds to India; no more were released.
In November 2025 the 11 surviving free-living birds were recaptured; all carried psittacine circovirus, an incurable disease, and once again none fly free.
In Belgium, Pairi Daiza hatched its first Spix’s chick that September, a future breeder.
To witness the Spix’s macaw is to hold a bird that exists because people kept it — and to ask whether they can let it go again.

stats.size: About 22 in long (55–57 cm) — little more than half a hyacinth macaw
stats.lifespan: 20–30 years in the wild; about 40 in captivity
stats.populationEstimate: None free-living since November 2025; about 350 in captivity
stats.populationAsOf: 2025 · per ICMBio figures reported by Mongabay and CNN Brasil
threats: Goat and sheep grazing of creek-side forest

reproduction.text: Breeding followed the rains, October to March, in caraibeira hollows — often ones woodpeckers had abandoned; the first pair to nest after the 2022 release laid clutches of three.

insight.text: The captive-bred birds released in 2022 followed flocks of wild blue-winged macaws, which acted as mentors — showing them, fruit by fruit, what a Spix's macaw eats in the Caatinga.

programs.title: Programa de Manejo Populacional da Ararinha-azul
programs.summary: Keeps Brazil’s studbook for Spix’s macaw and manages every captive bird as a single population — with the São Paulo Zoo, Loro Parque Fundación and partner centres such as Pairi Daiza — so that reintroduction in the Caatinga can resume.

programs.title: Project Spix's macaw
programs.summary: Breeds Spix's macaws at its conservation centre in Belgium, one of three breeding centres in the program alongside Germany and Brazil, and hatched its first chick in September 2025 to grow into a breeder.
